steps.title: Exercises with letters — toolkit
steps.intro: Four steps and a handful of facts — then plug in.

tables.title: The four steps
head: Step
What to do
rows: Check the leftmost digit and the size
Plug in numbers — or plug in the choices
Write \(10A+B\) and collect into a digit ratio: \(10A+B=4(A+B)\to6A=3B\to B=2A\): \(12,\ 24,\ 36,\ 48\)

tables.title: Facts to know
head: Fact
Example
rows: Two numbers, sum with more digits → leading digit is \(1\)
Carry: two numbers → \(0\) or \(1\); three or four numbers → up to \(2\) or \(3\)
\(5\times\) even ends in \(0\); \(5\times\) odd ends in \(5\)

tips: A bar on top (\(\overline{AB}\)) means: the digits of one number. \(\overline{AB}\) is not \(A\cdot B\).
Flip a subtraction into an addition, and a division into a multiplication.
Check whether the letters must be different digits.
Asked for one letter? Plug in the choices, starting from the middle one.
Plug in test numbers that are not alike. If two choices survive, try a third number.
A result is given → work the columns. "Always divisible by" with no result → plug in two numbers, or use the algebraic form.

steps.stem:
A, B, C and D represent digits. Given: \(\overline{BA}+\overline{DA}=\overline{CCA}\)
\(B+C+D=?\)
explanation: Write it vertically. Ones column: \(A+A\) ends in \(A\). Nothing carries into the ones column, so \(A=0\).
Two two-digit numbers give a three-digit number, so the leading digit is 1: \(C=1\).
Tens column: \(B+D\) (nothing carries in, because \(0+0=0\)) gives the tens digit 1 and carries 1 into the hundreds. So \(B+D=11\).

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent digits. Given: \(\overline{CB}\times B=\overline{AB}\)
Which of the following could be B?
explanation: Ones column: \(B\times B\) ends in \(B\). Only the special digits do this: \(0, 1, 5, 6\) (\(0\cdot0=0\), \(1\cdot1=1\), \(5\cdot5=25\), \(6\cdot6=36\)).
Choices (1) and (4) fail: \(4\cdot4=16\) and \(7\cdot7=49\).
Choice (2) fails: \(B=0\) makes the product \(0\), not a two-digit number.
Choice (3): \(B=5\) and \(C=1\) give \(15\times5=75\) ✓.

steps.stem: A and B represent nonzero digits. Which of the following necessarily divides \(\overline{AB}+\overline{BA}\)?
explanation: Plug in two different numbers. \(71+17=88\): it is not divisible by 3 or by 10, so choices (1) and (4) are out.
\(72+27=99\): it is not divisible by 4, so choice (3) is out. Only 11 is left.
Why it always works: \(\overline{AB}+\overline{BA}=(10A+B)+(10B+A)=11A+11B=11(A+B)\).

steps.title: Number facts for letter puzzles
steps.intro: Patterns that come back on the exam. Each one with an example.

tables.title: Facts
head: Fact
Example
rows: Multiples of \(99\): middle digit \(9\), outer digits add up to \(9\)
Units digit of a product: multiply only the units digits
Digits of a product: add the two counts, or one fewer
Largest with a digit sum: big digits on the left
Smallest with a digit sum: \(1\), then zeros, big digits on the right

tips: The units digit of \(2^{50}\): the cycle has 4 steps, \(50=4\cdot12+2\), so it ends like \(2^2\): \(4\).

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent digits. Given: \(\overline{BCA}+\overline{BC}=\overline{AAA}\)
\(C=?\)
explanation: Ones column: \(A+C\) ends in \(A\). Nothing carries into the ones column, so \(C=0\).
Check the tens: \(C+B=0+B\), so \(B=A\). For example: \(303+30=333\) ✓.

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent digits. Given: \(\overline{AAA}-46=\overline{BC}\)
\(B+C=?\)
explanation: Flip the subtraction into an addition: \(\overline{BC}+46=\overline{AAA}\).
Two two-digit numbers give a three-digit number, so the leading digit is 1: \(A=1\) and \(\overline{AAA}=111\).
\(A=1\), so \(\overline{AA}=11\). The other choices: \(\overline{BC}=65\), \(\overline{AC}=15\), \(\overline{AB}=16\).

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent digits. Given: \(\overline{AB}\times\overline{AB}=\overline{2CB}\)
Which of the following could be \(B-A\)?
explanation: Size first: \(14^2=196\) is too small, and \(18^2=324\) is too big. So \(\overline{AB}\) is 15, 16 or 17, and \(A=1\).
Ones column: \(B\times B\) ends in \(B\), so B is a special digit. Here \(B=5\) or \(B=6\) (\(17^2=289\) ends in 9, not in 7).

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent digits. Given: \(\frac{\overline{CBA}}{\overline{AA}}=17\)
\(A+B+C=?\)
explanation: Flip the division into a multiplication: \(\overline{AA}\times17=\overline{CBA}\).
Ones column: \(7\times A\) ends in \(A\). So \(6A\) ends in 0: \(A=0\) or \(A=5\). \(A=0\) is not possible, because \(\overline{AA}\) is a two-digit number. So \(A=5\).

steps.stem:
A, B, C and D represent different digits, and each of them is a prime number. Given: \(\overline{AB}+\overline{BC}=\overline{CD}\)
\(C=?\)
explanation: The prime digits are 2, 3, 5 and 7. There are four different letters, so each prime digit is used once.

Plug in the choices. \(C=5\): in the tens column, \(A+B\) (plus any carry) gives 5. Two different prime digits add up to at least \(2+3=5\), so nothing carries, and A and B are 2 and 3. Ones column: \(B+5=D\). \(B=2\) gives \(D=7\) ✓ (\(B=3\) would give 8). So \(A=3\). Check: \(32+25=57\) ✓.
The other choices fail. \(C=2\) or \(C=3\): the tens column needs \(A+B\) to be 2 or 3, but two different prime digits add up to at least 5.
\(C=7\): the ones column is \(B+7\). \(B=2\) gives 9 and \(B=3\) gives 10, but 9 and 0 are not prime. \(B=5\) gives 12: \(D=2\), 1 carries, and the tens \(A+5+1=7\) make \(A=1\), which is not prime.

steps.stem: x is a two-digit number. x is equal to the cube of its units digit plus 4 times the sum of its digits. What is the tens digit of x?
explanation: Plug in the choices for the tens digit T. Call the units digit U, so \(x=10T+U\).
The other choices fail: \(T=4\) gives \(U^3+3U=24\), \(T=7\) gives \(42\), \(T=5\) gives \(30\). But \(U^3+3U\) is \(0, 4, 14, 36, 76, \ldots\) — never one of them.
Algebraic form: \(10T+U=U^3+4T+4U\), so \(6T=U^3+3U\) — the same test.

steps.stem:
A and B represent digits. Given: \(\overline{2A6}+\overline{B8}=\overline{3A4}\)
\(B=?\)
explanation: Ones column: \(6+8=14\). Write 4 and carry 1 into the tens.
Tens column: \(A+B+1\) ends in \(A\). So \(B+1\) ends in 0: \(B+1=10\) and \(B=9\). This carries 1 again.
Hundreds column: \(2+1=3\) ✓.
The trap is \(B=0\): it forgets the carry. Check with \(A=5\): \(256+98=354\) ✓.

steps.stem: A, B and C represent digits, and \(A>C>0\). Which of the following could be the value of \(\overline{ABC}-\overline{CBA}\)?
explanation: \(\overline{ABC}-\overline{CBA}=99(A-C)\), so the result is a multiple of 99.
Multiples of 99 up to 891 have middle digit 9, and their outer digits add up to 9: \(198, 297, 396, 495, \ldots\)
\(459\), \(484\) and \(540\) do not have middle digit 9. \(495=99\cdot5\) ✓.

steps.stem: A and B represent digits. Which of the following could be the value of \(\overline{A3}\times\overline{B7}\)?
explanation: Units digit: only the units digits decide. \(3\cdot7=21\), so the product ends in 1. Choice (3) is out.
Size: the smallest product is \(13\cdot17=221\) and the largest is \(93\cdot97=9021\). So \(91\) is too small and \(10{,}001\) is too big.

steps.stem: A represents a nonzero digit. The three-digit number \(\overline{AAA}\) is necessarily divisible by which of the following?
explanation: \(\overline{AAA}=111A=3\cdot37\cdot A\), so it is always divisible by 37 (and by 3).
The others fail for \(A=1\): 111 is not divisible by 9, 2 or 5.

steps.stem: A is a three-digit number and B is a five-digit number. Which of the following is true about \(A+B\)?
choices: It can only be a five-digit number.
It can be a five-digit or a six-digit number.
It can only be a six-digit number.
It can be a four-digit or a five-digit number.
explanation: Smallest sum: \(100+10{,}000=10{,}100\) (five digits). Largest sum: \(999+99{,}999=100{,}998\) (six digits).
So \(A+B\) can be a five-digit or a six-digit number.

steps.stem:
A and B represent nonzero digits. Given: \(\overline{AB}-\overline{BA}=45\)
\(A-B=?\)
explanation: \(\overline{AB}-\overline{BA}=9(A-B)\).

steps.stem: A two-digit number is 7 times the sum of its digits. Its tens digit is 6. What is its units digit?
explanation: Plug in the choices: \(63=7\cdot(6+3)\) ✓.

The others fail: \(61
e7\cdot7\), \(66
e7\cdot12\), \(69
e7\cdot15\).
Algebraic form: \(60+b=7(6+b)\), so \(18=6b\) and \(b=3\).
Method 2 · Words, no columns: write the number as \(10A+B\) and collect. \(10A+B=7(A+B)\), so \(3A=6B\) and \(A=2B\). The tens digit is \(6\), so the units digit is \(3\).

steps.stem:
X, Y and Z represent consecutive digits, and \(X<Y<Z\). Given: \(X+Y+Z=\overline{1Y}\)
What is \(X+Y+Z\)?
explanation: Three consecutive digits: the sum is 3 times the middle one, \(3Y\).
\(\overline{1Y}=10+Y\), so \(3Y=10+Y\). Therefore \(2Y=10\) and \(Y=5\).
The digits are 4, 5 and 6, and the sum is \(15=\overline{1Y}\) ✓.

Or plug in the choices: the sum ends in Y and equals \(3Y\). Only \(15=3\cdot5\) works (\(12
e3\cdot2\), \(21
e3\cdot1\), \(18
e3\cdot8\)).

steps.stem:
A and B represent digits, and \(B\ne0\). Given: \(\overline{BBBBBB}\div\overline{BBB}=\overline{A00A}\)
\(A=?\)
explanation: It works for every B: \(\overline{BBBBBB}=111{,}111\cdot B\) and \(\overline{BBB}=111\cdot B\), so the quotient is always \(1001\). Check: \(444{,}444\div444=1001\) ✓.

steps.stem:
A and B represent different nonzero digits. Given: \(\overline{AB}\times6=\overline{4B0}\)
\(A-B=?\)
explanation: Ones column: \(6\times B\) ends in 0. B is not 0, so \(B=5\) (\(6\cdot5=30\)).
Then \(\overline{4B0}=450\), and \(\overline{AB}=450\div6=75\). So \(A=7\).

steps.stem:
A and B represent nonzero digits. Given: \(\overline{AB}\times B=\overline{B9}\)
\(A+B=?\)
explanation: Ones column: \(B\times B\) ends in 9. \(3\cdot3=9\) and \(7\cdot7=49\), so \(B=3\) or \(B=7\).
\(B=7\): \(\overline{A7}\times7\) is at least \(17\times7=119\) — too big for a two-digit result. So \(B=3\).
\(\overline{A3}\times3=39\), so \(\overline{A3}=13\) and \(A=1\). \(A+B=1+3=4\).

steps.stem:
n is the largest three-digit number whose digit sum is 9. m is the smallest three-digit number whose digit sum is 9.
\(n-m=?\)
explanation: Largest: put as much as possible in the leftmost digit: \(n=900\).
Smallest: the hundreds digit is at least 1. Then the smallest tens digit, 0, and the rest in the ones: \(m=108\).

steps.stem:
A and B represent digits. Given: \(\overline{4A}+\overline{4A}=\overline{9B}\)
What must A be at least?
explanation: Tens column: \(4+4=8\), but the tens digit of the result is 9. So 1 must carry from the ones column.
Ones column: \(A+A\) must be at least 10, so \(A\ge5\). \(A=5\) works: \(45+45=90\) ✓ (\(B=0\)).

steps.stem: X is a four-digit number. X is the sum of five three-digit numbers. Which of the following could be the thousands digit of X?
explanation: Five three-digit numbers add up to at most \(5\cdot999=4995\).
So the thousands digit of X is 1, 2, 3 or 4. Only 4 is a choice. Example: \(999+999+999+999+999=4995\).
The "leading digit 1" rule is only for the sum of two numbers.

steps.stem: A, B and C represent digits. What is the units digit of \(\overline{A7}\times\overline{B3}\times\overline{C9}\)?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: Only the units digits decide: \(7\cdot3=21\) ends in 1, and \(1\cdot9=9\).
So the units digit is 9, whatever A, B and C are. Check: \(17\cdot13\cdot19=4199\) ✓.

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent nonzero digits.
\(\frac{\overline{BA}+\overline{CB}+\overline{AC}}{A+B+C}=?\)
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: Algebraic form: each letter appears once in the tens and once in the ones. So the sum is \(11A+11B+11C=11(A+B+C)\), and the quotient is always 11.

steps.stem:
A, B, C and D represent consecutive digits, and \(A<B<C<D\). Given: \(k=\overline{AB}+\overline{CD}+53\)
Which of the following necessarily divides k?
explanation: Plug in \(A=1\): \(k=12+34+53=99\). 99 is not divisible by 7, so choice (4) is out.
Plug in \(A=2\): \(k=23+45+53=121=11\cdot11\). It is not divisible by 9 or by 3. Only 11 is left.
Algebraic form (always true): \(\overline{AB}=10A+(A+1)=11A+1\) and \(\overline{CD}=10(A+2)+(A+3)=11A+23\). So \(k=22A+77=11(2A+7)\).

steps.stem: X is a two-digit number whose units digit is 8. When we reverse the order of its digits, we get \(3(X+9)\). What is the sum of the digits of X?
explanation: Plug in the choices. The digit sum minus 8 is the tens digit: choice (1) gives \(X=38\), (2) gives \(X=18\), (3) gives \(X=58\), (4) gives \(X=78\).
\(X=18\): the reversed number is 81, and \(3(18+9)=81\) ✓.
The others fail. For example, \(X=38\): the reversed number is 83, but \(3(38+9)=141\).
Method 2 · Words, no columns: \(X=10A+8\), and the reversed number is \(80+A\). So \(80+A=3(10A+8+9)=30A+51\), which gives \(29A=29\) and \(A=1\).
\(X=18\), and the sum of its digits is \(9\).

steps.stem:
A and B represent nonzero digits. \(\overline{AB}\) is a two-digit prime number. The sum of its digits is 5 times its units digit.
\(A+B=?\)
explanation: \(A+B=5B\), so \(A=4B\). The options are 41 and 82.
82 is not prime: \(82=2\cdot41\). So \(\overline{AB}=41\) and \(A+B=5\).

steps.stem: Two three-digit numbers are made of the same three digits, in a different order. Their tens digits are equal. In one of the numbers, the hundreds digit is 7 more than the units digit. What is the difference between the two numbers?
explanation: Same digits and the same tens digit, so the hundreds digit and the units digit swap: the numbers are \(\overline{ABC}\) and \(\overline{CBA}\).
\(\overline{ABC}-\overline{CBA}=99(A-C)=99\cdot7=693\).

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent consecutive digits, and \(A<B<C\). D represents a digit. Given: \(\overline{ABC}+\overline{AAA}=\overline{D00}\)
\(A=?\)
explanation: Ones column: \(C+A\) ends in 0. \(C=A+2\), so \(2A+2\) ends in 0: \(A=4\) or \(A=9\). \(A=9\) is not possible, because \(C=A+2\) must be a digit. So \(A=4\), and 1 carries.
Then \(B=5\) and \(C=6\). Tens column: \(5+4+1=10\), so it ends in 0 ✓, and 1 carries again. Hundreds column: \(4+4+1=9\), so \(D=9\).

steps.stem:
A and B represent different nonzero digits. Given: \(\overline{AB}+B=\overline{BA}\)
\(B=?\)
explanation: Tens column: A plus the carry gives B. A and B are different, so the carry is 1 and \(B=A+1\).
Ones column: \(B+B=10+A\) (it carries 1). With \(A=B-1\): \(2B=10+B-1\), so \(B=9\) and \(A=8\).
Check: \(89+9=98\) ✓. (Or plug in the choices: only \(B=9\) works.)

steps.stem:
A and B represent different digits. Given: \(\overline{1A}\times B=\overline{8B}\)
Which of the following could be A?
explanation: Plug in the choices. \(A=7\): \(17\times B\) must be in the 80s, so \(B=5\): \(17\times5=85=\overline{8B}\) ✓.
\(A=9\): \(19\times4=76\) and \(19\times5=95\) — never in the 80s. \(A=4\): \(14\times6=84\), which ends in 4, not in \(B=6\). \(A=3\): \(13\times6=78\) and \(13\times7=91\) — never in the 80s.

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent digits. Given: \(\overline{ABC}-\overline{BBB}=297\)
\(A-C=?\)
explanation: Flip it into an addition: \(\overline{BBB}+297=\overline{ABC}\).
Tens column: \(B+9\) must end in \(B\). That works only with a carry of 1 from the ones: \(B+9+1=B+10\) ✓, and 1 carries into the hundreds.
Ones column: \(B+7\) carries 1, so \(C=B+7-10=B-3\). Hundreds column: \(B+2+1=A\), so \(A=B+3\).

steps.stem:
A represents a digit. Given: \(\overline{A8}+\overline{A8}+\overline{A8}=\overline{1A4}\)
\(A=?\)
explanation: Ones column: \(8+8+8=24\). Write 4 and carry 2 (three numbers can carry more than 1).
Tens column: \(A+A+A+2\) ends in \(A\). So \(2A+2\) ends in 0: \(A=4\) or \(A=9\).
\(A=9\): \(27+2=29\) carries 2, so the hundreds digit would be 2, not 1 ✗. \(A=4\): \(12+2=14\), tens digit 4, carry 1 ✓.

steps.stem:
A, B and C represent digits. Given: \(\overline{AA}\times\overline{BB}=\overline{ACA}\)
Which of the following could be \(\overline{AA}\)?
explanation: Try each choice with the smallest BB, 11:
\(55\times11=605\), \(66\times11=726\) and \(88\times11=968\): the first and last digits are different ✗. \(44\times11=484\) ✓ (\(A=4\), \(C=8\)).
A bigger BB does not help 55, 66 or 88: \(55\times22=1210\), \(66\times22=1452\) and \(88\times22=1936\) have four digits.

steps.stem: A and B represent different digits from 1 to 8. When \(\overline{AB}\) is divided by 11, the remainder is less than 4. Which of the following cannot be A?
explanation: Plug in the choices. For \(A=8\), \(\overline{AB}\) is one of 81, 82, 83, 84, 85, 86, 87. \(88=8\cdot11\), so these leave the remainders 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 — never less than 4. So A cannot be 8.

steps.stem:
A and B represent nonzero digits. Given: \(\overline{1AB}-\overline{BA}=\overline{B2}\)
\(A+B=?\)
explanation: Flip it into an addition: \(\overline{BA}+\overline{B2}=\overline{1AB}\).
Ones column: \(A+2\) ends in \(B\). If it carried, B would be 0 or 1, and the tens \(B+B+1\) could not reach 10. So nothing carries and \(B=A+2\).
Plug in the choices: \(A+B=14\) gives \(A=6\) and \(B=8\). Check: \(168-86=82=\overline{B2}\) ✓.
